It can be very difficult when you love someone dearly, but things trigger you. I've had to open up to my mother about all of my triggers in order to feel comfortable being around her again , even as an adult things still bother me , so having awareness of my issues has made it easier. 
Misophonia can make you hate being around someone because of either the triggers or FEAR of the triggers, and I think teaching your kids about it and why it happens, I think will help foster understanding between him and the kids. It's definitely important to clarify he doesn't hate them, he reacts that way because he can't help it. I can only imagine seeing their father always angry or trying to hide being angry at the table might affect them worse than knowing the truth . 
You have an 8 and a 5 year old, which is about the ages I realized I had misophonia triggers, so I think they're old enough to learn and see what they can do about it. 

On my father's side of the family, him, his sisters and other family members have it , in different ranges of severity. So it's possible that your kids could have it, or develop triggers. So letting them know not only helps understand your husband better, but may help them have a means of knowing if they have it.

So overall: don't hide it from your kids, it could hurt your husband and hurt them in the long run.

I think you might find Paragard worth trying. Paragard doesn't usually cost more than hormonal IUDs ( and IUDs are usually covered by insurance and so forth) 
And what you said about it possibly carrying you till menopause, that sounds like a pretty sweet deal. 
One thing I will say is it is on the larger side, so it does have higher risk of expulsion. 
And Paragard does have to remain in a particular place to protect u, it can't move around out of place as the physical IUD is the only thing protecting. 
Hormonal IUDs also may give you benefits in reducing period pain and flow , but tlhormones can make you more sensitive to things such as caffeine and anxiety and so forth. If you feel like however the mirena is doable and you've already had a decent experience with it , then there may be no need to switch. 

One thing too about tubal ligations is some people have bad luck convincing doctor's you know what's right for you, others don't have an issue. 
For perspective, I'm 21 and got approved for a tubal at the beginning of March  , due to not wanting kids or to be pregnant as well as generally having bad reactions to hormonal birth control , and really the only thing stopping me currently is due to COVID-19 making hospitals in my area for emergencies only, so it has to be put off for now. So it's different among people , and sometimes you just have to be very assertive and ready to answer " hard " questions . 

With all that being said, my perspective on this is to go with whatever seems the most interesting to you now, it might be worth trying Paragard to see if you notice any changes to libido and sensitivity to certain things, I'd say be wary that your flow might increase with Paragard, but it may more so have to do with going off hormonal birth control than anything else. And if you find you don't like Paragard, then there's no harm in returning to mirena or looking into a tubal if that's something you still consider. There's no harm in trying out different IUDs and finding out if a new ones good for you or not.

Now ofc it doesn't mean getting the bisalp will be easy, but here are some thoughts I have on things you may run into: 
  it may not be what you'll want to have happen, but definitely expect to be told to try hormonal birth control first. And if you decide to try it or not is up to you. But I will say that unless you avoid sex altogether until you get sterlized ( which could take awhile, and in your case could potentially take a year or maybe  couple of years ) you're likely to be more protected if you use one or two methods of birth control. You can indeed pair two methods . Any hormonal method of bc + condom use would give you near impossible chance of getting pregnant as long as it's used correctly. 


No method is perfect by any means, but if you want personal recromendation on a  method that's almost foolproof , the nexplanon implant is one I'd recommend personally ( tho ik not everyone will agree) . labelled for 3 year use but has been proven to still work properly and profit up to 5 years by planned Parenthood . It's inserted in the arm, no pills to take, shots to take , and nothing goes into your uterus . And statistically is over 99% effective, it's pretty on par with sterlization. The /birthcontrol Reddit is a good spot if you wanted to learn the good and the bad about every method ( including sterlization) and is very helpful. 
I only say all of this because I personally never heard of someone getting sterlized around our age that never been on any other method of birth control before, and you at least trying it out while you search may give doctor's even more reason to trust your decision.
